articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's Short-Term Rental Fight Heads to Summer Showdown
articles.dek: Three years of failed ordinances, a split commission, and a Perdido Key neighborhood at war with itself. What happens when the board votes in June could reshape the beach economy—or punt the issue another year.
brief: Escambia County Commission will vote June 18 on a short-term rental ordinance that has failed twice since 2023
Perdido Key residents remain sharply divided between property rights advocates and those seeking neighborhood preservation
The outcome could establish Florida's strictest local STR regulations or leave the unincorporated coast largely unregulated
articles.body:
The house at 14502 Perdido Key Drive sits dark most weeknights. On Fridays, cars with Louisiana and Alabama plates fill the driveway and spill onto the narrow shoulder. Music carries across the dunes until 2 a.m. By Sunday afternoon, the renters are gone. The cycle repeats.

Linda Harwell has lived next door for 23 years. She keeps a notebook by her kitchen window. Dates. License plates. Noise complaints filed. Code enforcement responses received. The notebook is nearly full.

"I bought a home," Harwell said. "They bought a hotel and put it in the middle of my neighborhood."

Three streets over, Mike Castellano manages 14 short-term rental properties for out-of-state owners. He disputes Harwell's framing. "These homes generate $40,000 a year in tourist development taxes each. They employ cleaners, landscapers, pool techs. This is Perdido Key's economy. Full stop."

On June 18, the Escambia County Commission will vote on an ordinance that attempts to reconcile these positions. It is the third such attempt since 2023. The previous two failed—one withdrawn before a vote, one defeated 3-2. County staff have spent 14 months drafting the current proposal, which runs 47 pages and includes registration requirements, occupancy limits, parking standards and a complaint-tracking system.

The vote will likely be close. And the losing side will likely sue.

What the ordinance actually does

The proposed Short-Term Rental Regulatory Program would require all STR operators in unincorporated Escambia County to register annually with the county and pay a $250 fee. Properties would be inspected for life-safety compliance before approval. Operators would need to designate a local responsible party available within 60 minutes to respond to complaints.

Occupancy would be capped at two persons per bedroom plus two additional guests, with a hard maximum of 12 regardless of bedroom count. Parking requirements mandate one off-street space per bedroom. Quiet hours between 10 p.m. and 8 a.m. would be enforceable through the county's existing noise ordinance.

A three-strike system would allow the county to revoke registrations for properties with verified violations. Unregistered rentals would face fines of $500 per day.

The ordinance applies only to unincorporated areas—primarily Perdido Key, Innerarity Point and portions of Pensacola Beach outside the Santa Rosa Island Authority's jurisdiction.

The coalition that can't hold

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh represents District 1, which includes most of Perdido Key. He has been the ordinance's most vocal champion on the board since 2021. But his position has evolved.

"Three years ago I wanted a full moratorium," Bergosh said in a phone interview. "I've come to understand that's not legally defensible and probably not right anyway. What we're proposing now is reasonable regulation. It's what most of my constituents are asking for."

Bergosh points to a 2024 survey his office conducted of Perdido Key property owners. Of 1,847 responses, 62% supported some form of STR regulation. But the survey's methodology drew criticism—it was distributed primarily through homeowner association newsletters, potentially oversampling long-term residents.

Commissioner Steven Barry, whose District 5 includes no coastal areas, has consistently opposed regulation. He frames the issue in property rights terms. "If you own a home, you should be able to rent it. Period. The county shouldn't be in the business of telling people how to use their property."

Barry also questions enforcement costs. County staff estimate the program would require three new code enforcement officers and one administrative position, totaling approximately $340,000 annually. Registration fees would offset roughly half that amount, leaving taxpayers to cover the difference.

"We're going to spend $170,000 a year to make Linda Harwell's neighbors quieter," Barry said. "That's not a responsible use of public money."

The remaining three commissioners—Lumon May, Robert Bender and Doug Underhill—have not committed publicly. May and Bender voted against the 2024 proposal. Underhill, who returned to the board after a two-year absence, has requested additional data on enforcement in other Florida counties before deciding.

The legal landscape

Florida law significantly constrains what counties can do. A 2011 statute prohibited local governments from banning short-term rentals outright. A 2014 amendment allowed regulation of "life safety" issues—fire codes, occupancy limits, parking—but barred restrictions based purely on rental duration or frequency.

The line between permissible safety regulation and impermissible rental restriction remains contested. Several Florida counties have faced legal challenges to their STR ordinances. Brevard County's registration program survived a 2022 court challenge. Walton County's more aggressive approach, which included mandatory 30-day gaps between rentals, was struck down in 2023.

Escambia's ordinance was drafted with these precedents in mind. County Attorney Alison Rogers said the proposal "threads the needle" by focusing exclusively on health, safety and nuisance issues. "We're not regulating the rental activity itself. We're regulating the impacts that rental activity creates."

Not everyone is convinced. The Florida Alliance for Vacation Rentals, an industry group, sent a letter to commissioners in April calling the proposed occupancy limits "a de facto ban dressed up as safety regulation." The group has not said whether it would pursue litigation if the ordinance passes.

Property rights advocates have their own legal concerns. A coalition of Perdido Key homeowners filed a formal complaint with the county in March arguing that certain STR properties constitute unpermitted commercial activity in residential zones. That complaint remains under review by the county attorney's office.

The numbers nobody agrees on

Depending on whom you ask, Perdido Key has between 800 and 2,400 active short-term rentals. The county does not track them directly. The low estimate comes from active Airbnb and VRBO listings compiled by a Pensacola-based data firm. The high estimate comes from the Escambia County Property Appraiser's office, which flags properties claiming homestead exemption that appear on rental platforms.

The gap matters. If 800 properties generate the revenue the tourist development council claims—roughly $32 million in direct visitor spending annually—then each rental averages $40,000. If 2,400 properties generate that revenue, the average drops to $13,333. The former figure suggests a concentrated economic driver worth protecting. The latter suggests a diffuse cottage industry that might not justify regulatory infrastructure.

Tourist Development Council Director Dana Sargent declined to comment on the discrepancy. Her office provided a statement noting that "short-term rentals are a significant component of Escambia County's tourism economy" without offering specific figures.

Property appraiser records show 847 properties in unincorporated Escambia County claimed homestead exemption in 2025 while also appearing on at least one major vacation rental platform. Claiming homestead exemption on a rental property is illegal under Florida law. Whether those listings represent active rentals or outdated profiles cannot be determined from available data.

What happens next

The June 18 meeting is scheduled to begin at 5:30 p.m. at the Ernie Lee Magaha Government Building in downtown Pensacola. Public comment will be open before the vote. Based on previous STR hearings, county staff expect the meeting to run past 9 p.m.

If the ordinance passes, registration requirements would take effect October 1. Property inspections would begin in January 2027. The three-strike enforcement system would go live the following July.

If it fails, Commissioner Bergosh has indicated he will not bring another proposal before the board. "At some point you accept that you don't have the votes," he said. "I'll have done what I could for my constituents. The rest is up to the state."

Several state legislators have proposed STR bills in recent sessions. None have passed. A 2025 proposal that would have established a statewide registration system died in committee. Industry groups opposed it as regulatory overreach. Municipal leagues opposed it as preemption of local control. The coalition against action proved broader than any coalition for it.

On Perdido Key, the status quo holds. Linda Harwell will keep her notebook. Mike Castellano will keep his properties booked. The cars will keep coming on Fridays. The music will keep playing until someone calls code enforcement or doesn't.

June 18 might change that. Or it might not.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The $40 Million Hole Downtown: Inside the Stalled Block 58 Project
articles.dek: The city sold the land. The developer made promises. Two years later, there's still a fence around dirt. A look at what went wrong and who's on the hook.
brief: Block 58, a city-owned parcel sold in 2024 for mixed-use development, remains an empty lot surrounded by chain-link fence
Developer Emerald Coast Urban Partners has missed multiple construction milestones and faces potential default on its agreement with the city
City officials now weighing whether to claw back the property or renegotiate terms amid questions about due diligence in the original sale
articles.body:
The fence went up in October 2024. Orange construction mesh. A sign promising 200 residential units, 40,000 square feet of retail, and a rooftop restaurant with views of Pensacola Bay. "Coming 2026," it said.

Twenty months later, the sign is sun-bleached and peeling. The fence is still there. So is the dirt.

Block 58—a half-acre city-owned parcel at the corner of Palafox and Main—was supposed to be the catalyst for downtown Pensacola's next chapter. Instead, it's become a monument to stalled ambition, disputed timelines, and increasingly pointed questions about how the city vets the developers it does business with.

The Sale

The Pensacola City Council voted 6-1 in March 2024 to sell Block 58 to Emerald Coast Urban Partners for $2.1 million. The price was below the $2.8 million appraisal, but the discount came with conditions: construction had to begin within 18 months, and the project had to include at least 15% workforce housing units.

Emerald Coast Urban Partners presented itself as a joint venture between a Miami-based development firm, Coastal Meridian Holdings, and local investors. The company's pitch included glossy renderings, letters of intent from two national restaurant chains, and a financing commitment from a regional bank.

Councilwoman Ann Hill cast the lone dissenting vote. She wanted more time to review the financing structure.

"We were told this was a sure thing," Hill said in an interview last week. "I asked for the bank commitment letter. I got a summary. Not the letter."

City records obtained through a public records request show the council received a two-page summary of the financing terms, not the 47-page commitment letter itself. The summary did not mention that the commitment was conditional on Emerald Coast securing a separate $12 million equity investment by December 2024.

That investment never materialized.

The Delays

By the terms of the purchase agreement, Emerald Coast was required to submit final architectural plans by September 2024 and break ground by September 2025. Neither deadline was met.

The company requested its first extension in August 2024, citing "supply chain complications" in finalizing design specifications. The city granted a 90-day extension without a public vote, as permitted under the agreement's administrative provisions.

A second extension request came in February 2025. This time, Emerald Coast cited difficulties securing the equity investment and requested 12 additional months. The council approved the extension 4-3 in a contentious meeting that drew roughly 60 residents to City Hall.

Marcus Bell, managing partner of Emerald Coast, assured the council the project remained viable.

"We are committed to Pensacola," Bell said at that meeting. "The capital markets have been challenging, but we have strong interest from institutional investors. We will deliver."

Public records show Bell made similar assurances in private emails to city staff throughout 2025. In a November 2025 email to Community Redevelopment Agency director Tom Hinton, Bell wrote that a "major Southeast regional investor" was prepared to close on the equity portion by January 2026.

January passed. No closing occurred.

Who Is Emerald Coast Urban Partners?

Emerald Coast Urban Partners was incorporated in Delaware in January 2024, two months before the Block 58 vote. It registered as a foreign LLC in Florida that same month.

The company's registered agent is a corporate services firm in Wilmington. Its principal address is a virtual office in Miami's Brickell district.

Coastal Meridian Holdings, the Miami firm listed as the majority partner, has completed two projects: a 48-unit apartment building in Hialeah and a mixed-use development in Fort Pierce that opened three years behind schedule and 40% over budget. The Fort Pierce project was the subject of a 2022 lawsuit by subcontractors alleging nonpayment. The suit was settled out of court.

The local investors in Emerald Coast have not been publicly identified. Bell declined to name them in an interview with The Flightline, citing confidentiality agreements.

"Our local partners are committed to this community and prefer to remain private," Bell said. "That's not unusual in development."

City Council President Sherri Myers said she was not aware of Coastal Meridian's history with the Fort Pierce project before the 2024 vote.

"That would have been useful information," Myers said. "I don't know why we didn't have it."

What the City Knew

The Flightline submitted a public records request for all due diligence materials the city compiled before the Block 58 sale. The response included 214 pages of documents.

The materials show city staff conducted a basic background check on Emerald Coast and its principals, including searches of court records and news archives. The search found no criminal records and no bankruptcy filings.

But the due diligence did not include a detailed review of Coastal Meridian's project history, financial audits, or interviews with officials in jurisdictions where the company had previously worked.

Former city attorney Jim Martin, who left his position in June 2025, signed off on the purchase agreement. In an email to the city manager dated February 2024, Martin wrote that the agreement's clawback provisions "provide adequate protection for the city's interests."

Those provisions allow the city to reclaim the property if the developer fails to meet construction milestones, but only after a 180-day cure period and binding arbitration. The process could take 18 months or more.

"The clawback is there, but it has teeth like a gummy bear," said Jennifer Walsh, a land-use attorney in private practice who reviewed the agreement at The Flightline's request. "Any experienced developer would know they have years of runway before facing real consequences."

The Current Impasse

The extended deadline for breaking ground passed on February 28, 2026. No construction has begun.

On March 15, the city sent Emerald Coast a formal notice of default, triggering the 180-day cure period. The company has until September 11 to either begin construction or face arbitration proceedings.

In a written statement to The Flightline, Bell said the company is "actively engaged in finalizing our capital stack" and expects to announce a new financing partner "in the coming weeks."

"Block 58 will be built," the statement read. "We remain confident in the project's viability and our commitment to downtown Pensacola."

City staff members are less optimistic. In interviews, two officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly said they expect the project to enter arbitration.

"We're preparing for that outcome," one official said. "The question is what happens after. Do we get the land back in six months? A year? Two years? And then we start over."

The Cost of Waiting

Block 58 sits at what urban planners call a "gateway location"—visible from Palafox Street, walking distance to the bay, surrounded by recent investments in streetscaping and public art.

The empty lot sends a message to visitors and residents alike. To some, it says downtown Pensacola is still a work in progress. To others, it says the city can't close deals.

Adjacent property owners have noticed.

Maria Santos owns a hair salon on the opposite corner. She signed a lease in 2024 partly because of Block 58.

"They told us this building was coming, restaurants, apartments, foot traffic," Santos said. "I based my business plan on that. Now I have a view of dirt and fence."

Her rent has increased 12% since she opened. Her foot traffic has not.

Downtown property values have continued to rise overall, according to Escambia County Property Appraiser data, but the Block 58 parcel itself was reassessed downward in 2025. The city received $2.1 million for land now appraised at $1.95 million—though that valuation assumes eventual development.

If the city claws back the property, it will have spent two years with no tax revenue, no development, and significant staff time managing a dispute. The legal costs for arbitration could reach $200,000 or more, according to estimates from the city attorney's office.

What Happens Next

The council will discuss Block 58 in a closed-door session next week, according to the posted agenda. State law permits such sessions when litigation is pending or anticipated.

Three council members—Hill, Delarian Wiggins, and P.C. Wu—have called publicly for the city to pursue clawback immediately and not entertain further extensions. Myers has said she wants to hear from the city attorney before taking a position.

Mayor D.C. Reeves has been notably quiet. His office did not respond to requests for comment.

The September deadline looms. If Emerald Coast cannot demonstrate meaningful progress, the city will face a choice: continue waiting on a partner that has missed every deadline, or start over with two years lost and a legal fight ahead.

Either way, the fence stays up for now.

The sign promising 2026 delivery has been taken down. No one has replaced it.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola Braces for Base Realignment Rumors as Pentagon Review Begins
articles.dek: The Defense Department's latest infrastructure audit has local leaders nervous. The Cradle of Naval Aviation has survived BRAC before—but this time the calculus is different.
brief: Pentagon launches comprehensive infrastructure review that could trigger base realignment recommendations by early 2027
NAS Pensacola employs over 23,000 military and civilian personnel, generating an estimated $5.1 billion annual regional economic impact
Local officials and Florida delegation members are already mobilizing to protect the 200-year-old installation
articles.body:
The gates at NAS Pensacola opened at 0500 Tuesday morning like they have for more than a century. Flight instructors gathered in ready rooms. Student naval aviators walked toward the flight line. The National Naval Aviation Museum sat quiet in the predawn darkness, its collection of 150 aircraft waiting for the first tour groups.

Three hundred miles north in Washington, Pentagon officials had just released a 47-page document that could reshape all of it.

The Defense Department's Infrastructure Capacity Review, announced Monday, directs military branches to identify "excess capacity and consolidation opportunities" across domestic installations. Defense Secretary Marcus Webb called it "a responsible examination of how we maintain readiness while being good stewards of taxpayer resources."

For Pensacola, those words land differently than they might in other Navy towns. The Cradle of Naval Aviation has weathered Base Realignment and Closure rounds before—in 1993, 1995, and 2005. Each time, the installation emerged intact. But military planners and local officials acknowledge that historical significance alone no longer guarantees survival.

'Different Pressures Now'

"Every base thinks it's essential. Every community believes its installation is untouchable," said retired Rear Adm. Catherine Briggs, who commanded Naval Education and Training Command at NAS Pensacola from 2018 to 2021. "The ones that survive are the ones that prove it with numbers."

The numbers for NAS Pensacola tell a complicated story. The base employs approximately 16,000 military personnel and 7,400 civilians, according to Navy figures from fiscal year 2025. The Haas Center at the University of West Florida estimates the installation's total regional economic impact at $5.1 billion annually, making it Escambia County's largest employer by a significant margin.

But the base also sits on aging infrastructure. A 2024 Navy facilities assessment identified $890 million in deferred maintenance across the installation, including outdated training facilities, deteriorating hangars, and a seawall system that requires constant attention. Hurricane Sally in 2020 caused an estimated $400 million in damage. Much of that has been repaired. Some of it hasn't.

"The physical plant is a vulnerability," said Marcus Chen, a defense analyst at the Center for Strategic and International Studies who studies military infrastructure. "When you're competing against newer facilities in less hurricane-prone areas, you have to make a stronger case for why investment here makes sense."

Mission Consolidation Questions

What makes this review different from previous rounds is the Pentagon's explicit interest in training consolidation. The document specifically mentions "aviation training pipeline efficiencies" as an area of focus.

NAS Pensacola serves as the hub for initial naval flight training. Every Navy, Marine Corps, and Coast Guard aviator passes through the installation at some point in their training. The Naval Aviation Schools Command oversees ground-based instruction. The Training Air Wing Six operates T-6B Texan II aircraft for primary flight training.

But primary training also occurs at NAS Whiting Field in Milton, NAS Corpus Christi in Texas, and Vance Air Force Base in Oklahoma through joint agreements. Advanced training happens elsewhere entirely. Critics of the current system argue that geographic dispersion creates inefficiencies.

"There's been talk for years about whether you could consolidate primary training into fewer locations," said James Callahan, a former Naval Air Systems Command official who now consults for defense contractors. "Pensacola's advantage has always been the concentration of support functions—the museum, the historical ties, the community relationship. Whether that's enough in a constrained budget environment is the question."

Navy officials declined to comment on specific installations under review. A spokesperson for Naval Education and Training Command referred questions to the Pentagon.

Political Response

Florida's congressional delegation moved quickly after the announcement. Sen. Rick Scott released a statement Monday evening calling NAS Pensacola "irreplaceable" and pledging to "fight any effort to diminish its role." Rep. Matt Gaetz, whose district includes the installation, posted on social media that he had requested a briefing from Navy leadership.

Gov. Ron DeSantis's office said the governor spoke with defense officials Tuesday morning but declined to characterize the conversation.

At the local level, Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh said the county commission would discuss the review at its June 5 meeting. "We need a coordinated response," Bergosh said. "This isn't the time for individual voices. This is the time for one message."

Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves said his office had already been in contact with the Greater Pensacola Chamber and FloridaWest Economic Development Alliance about forming a unified advocacy effort. "We've done this before. We know how to make the case," Reeves said. "But we also can't be complacent."

History and Uncertainty

The base's history cuts both ways in these discussions. NAS Pensacola was established in 1914, making it the first naval air station in the United States. The Blue Angels have been headquartered here since 1949. The National Naval Aviation Museum draws nearly a million visitors annually.

That heritage creates political complications for anyone proposing closure or significant realignment. It also creates assumptions that may not hold.

"Historical significance is a factor, but it's not a deciding factor," said Briggs, the retired rear admiral. "Mare Island had history. The Philadelphia Navy Yard had history. They closed anyway because the mission requirements changed."

The Pentagon review is expected to produce preliminary recommendations by February 2027. Any actual base closures would require Congressional approval through a formal BRAC process—something Congress has repeatedly declined to authorize since 2005.

But realignment short of closure remains possible through administrative action. Functions can be moved. Personnel can be reassigned. Training pipelines can be restructured without formally shuttering a gate.

At the National Naval Aviation Museum Tuesday afternoon, a group of elementary school students from Mobile filed past the NC-4 flying boat that made the first transatlantic crossing in 1919. A docent explained that it departed from right here, from this base, more than a hundred years ago.

Outside, T-6 turboprops traced patterns in the sky above the runway. Student pilots learning the same skills in the same airspace that has produced naval aviators since Woodrow Wilson was president.

Whether that continues is no longer a settled question.
